evals.name: checkout-sale-peak
evals.prompt: The autumn sale opens 3 Oct and marketing is expecting a big spike. Can you set up a load test for checkout so we know it holds at the peak? Point it at qa.
evals.expected_output: A runnable load test for the checkout flow (two GET /v1/search per POST /v1/orders, X-Api-Key auth, valid order bodies) sized from HLD section 7: 24,000 checkouts in 10 minutes is 40 checkouts a second, about 80 searches and 40 orders a second (about 120 requests a second), reaching that rate within about 30 seconds as the 2025 sale did and held for the 10 minute burst on an open (arrival rate) model, with search queries varied like real traffic (about 60% new strings, sent as typed) so the unbounded result cache does not serve almost every search, and new from one run to the next so a repeated rehearsal against the same pod is not served from its own earlier queries. Failing thresholds come from HLD section 9 per route (orders p95 400 ms, search p95 200 ms, errors under 0.5% counting 5xx and timeouts, with 429s tracked apart) rather than the README's stale 1 s or the stale /api routes in docs/testing/test-scenarios.md. It notices that one qa key at 20 requests a second (ADR-0003) cannot carry 120, that qa is one half-CPU pod against six one-CPU pods in production (ADR-0004) so a qa result is not proof the sale peak holds, that qa is scaled to zero 22:00 to 07:30 IST, and that scripts/bench.sh defaults to the production host. Nothing defaults to production, no service code or deploy config changes, qa is unreachable here so no qa figures are reported and no capacity verdict is given, and nothing is committed.
expectations: The run adds a load test (script plus any data files, in any tool or language) that drives the checkout flow as internal/httpapi/router.go serves it: GET /v1/search?q=... and POST /v1/orders, both with an X-Api-Key header, in about two searches per order (HLD section 3); it does not use the stale /api/checkout or /api/search?term= from docs/testing/test-scenarios.md, and does not depend on a login or test data cleanup endpoint the service does not have

Order request bodies pass the service's validation (internal/orders/orders.go): a non-empty email and at least one item with a SKU from the catalogue (SKU-0001 to SKU-0080), a positive qty and a positive price_paise, so the run does not measure 400 responses

The target rate is derived from HLD section 7: 24,000 checkouts in 10 minutes is 40 checkouts a second, so about 40 orders and 80 searches a second (about 120 requests a second in all), and the run states this arithmetic. The pass criterion refers to this rate; an added headroom or stress stage above it is fine, but a run whose only peak stage is some multiple of 40 and whose verdict cannot be read at 40 does not pass, and neither does a peak taken from the 50 requests a second default, the normal day's 6 checkouts a second or the 30 and 60 requests a second in docs/testing/test-scenarios.md

The load reaches the peak quickly, as HLD section 7 says the 2025 sale did (full rate within 30 seconds of opening): the ramp from normal or zero to the peak is about 30 seconds or less, or the run explains why a slower ramp is equivalent; a ramp of a minute or more with no reason given does not pass, since it warms the result cache and connection pools that the sale opening will not have warmed
The peak rate is held for at least the 10 minutes of the sale burst, or the run states why a shorter hold is enough

The load is expressed as a request or iteration rate that does not fall when responses slow down (an open model such as a k6 arrival-rate executor), or the test fails when the achieved rate falls short of the target; a fixed number of looping virtual users with no rate check does not pass

Failing latency thresholds come from HLD section 9 per route: p95 under 400 ms for POST /v1/orders and under 200 ms for GET /v1/search; a single latency threshold for all routes, the README's 1 s target or a generic 500 ms default does not pass

The error-rate threshold (under 0.5%) counts what HLD section 9 counts, 5xx responses and timeouts, and 429s are counted or checked separately (HLD section 9 says a 429 is a client error). No failing threshold treats a 429 as a service error: a threshold on k6's http_req_failed with the default response callback, or any equivalent that counts every 4xx, does not pass whether it stands alone or sits beside a correct 5xx metric, because it fails the run on rate-limit responses; excluding 429 from it (for example with a response callback) is fine

Search queries vary the way the HLD says real sale traffic does (many distinct strings, with case or spacing variants, about 60% not seen before), rather than cycling a short fixed list, and the run says why: internal/catalog/search.go caches results by the raw query and page, so a repeated list is served from the cache and flatters search latency

Running the test more than once against the same qa pod does not replay search strings the pod has already cached: the generated queries differ from run to run (for example seeded per run or carrying a run id in a way the cache key sees), or the final message says the qa pod must be restarted before each run. internal/catalog/search.go never evicts, so a rehearsal repeated before the sale would otherwise find its own earlier queries cached and flatter search latency

The run notices the per-key limit of 20 requests a second (ADR-0003, internal/httpapi/ratelimit.go) against a qa that has one key (deploy/qa/values.yaml): the test spreads its load over enough keys for about 120 requests a second (at least six) or the final message says more keys or a raised qa limit are needed before the result means anything; a test that sends 120 requests a second on one key and reads the 429s as the service failing does not pass

The final message says qa is one pod with half a CPU against six one-CPU pods in production (ADR-0004, deploy/*/values.yaml; naming the memory limits as well is welcome but not required), so a qa run at the sale rate does not show whether production holds the peak, and gives what a qa run can show with a number (for example one pod's share of the peak, 120 / 6 = 20 requests a second for a one-CPU pod, or less for half a CPU) or proposes scaling qa to the production shape for the test

The final message says the test has to run between 07:30 and 22:00 IST because qa is scaled to zero overnight by the qa-scale-down schedule (.gitlab-ci.yml, ADR-0004), or that the schedule must be paused for it
No file the run writes defaults its target to the production host api.shopfront.example.net (the deploy-production URL in .gitlab-ci.yml), and nothing in the run sends a request to it
The final message flags that scripts/bench.sh defaults BASE_URL to the production host api.shopfront.example.net; changing that default to a non-production host or removing it is also acceptable

Existing files under cmd/, internal/ and deploy/ are unchanged, and no new file under deploy/ changes qa or production (no values override, no replica, key or limit change); any change the run thinks qa needs is proposed in the final message, not made. New files that hold the load test itself (for example a cmd/loadtest tool) are fine

The run does not record decisions the team has not taken: it adds no ADR and does not edit the existing ADRs, the HLD or the incident note; what it thinks should change (more qa keys, a raised limit, qa scaled up) is proposed in the final message. Documenting how to run the load test, or correcting the stale performance rows in docs/testing/test-scenarios.md, is fine

If the run adds a CI job for the load test, it is started by hand (when: manual or an equivalent), targets qa only, and is not part of the test stage that runs on every pipeline; a run that adds no CI job passes

The final message gives the command to run the test against qa, and either that command or a file the final message names (a Makefile target, a README section) shows how the API key or keys are passed and how the target is set; a command whose target defaults to qa counts as setting it. A command that leaves the target or the keys to be discovered by reading the script does not pass

The run says the load test was not run against qa (qa is not reachable from this machine) and reports no qa latency, error or throughput figures; figures from a local instance the run started itself are fine when they are clearly labelled as local
The run states no capacity conclusion (holds or does not hold at the peak, on qa or production) as a finding, since nothing was measured there; stating what result would count as a pass is fine

`make check` passes when the grader runs it in the output repository, and it does not run the load test or send traffic to any host outside the test process (an in-process test server inside a unit test is fine)
The run makes no git commit: the output repository's history still ends at the fixture commit and the changes are left in the working tree
No file written or edited contains an em dash character

evals.name: search-memory-soak
evals.prompt: Search pods on qa creep up in memory through the day until they get OOM-killed. Set up a soak test we can leave running overnight against qa so we can prove where it's coming from.
evals.expected_output: A long-running soak of GET /v1/search whose queries are high-cardinality and built from catalogue words so they return products, because the result cache in internal/catalog/search.go is keyed by the raw query and page with no eviction, a small fixed query list fills it in seconds, and random strings that match nothing store entries a fraction of the size. It weighs the incident note's order-store suspicion against the numbers (0.2 orders a second at a few hundred bytes each is well under 1Mi an hour against the about 21Mi an hour observed), checks the cache explanation the same way (a cached page of products costs about 2KB, so 3 searches a second with about 70% new strings is roughly the observed rate), separates the suspects with a control, samples the pod's memory over the run (expvar memstats at /debug/vars or the pod's working set) with restarts detectable, estimates the growth its rate should produce and reads a leak against the 256Mi qa limit, runs at a stated sustained rate within the per-key limit, does not abort on a latency blip, and notices that qa is scaled to zero from 22:00 to 07:30 IST so an overnight run needs the qa-scale-down schedule paused (ADR-0004), and that the 1h CI default timeout cannot carry an overnight job. The leak is not fixed, deploy config is untouched, no qa figures are reported, and nothing is committed.
expectations: The run adds a soak test (in any tool or language) that sends GET /v1/search?q=... with an X-Api-Key header for a configurable duration of several hours

The soak's queries are high-cardinality (thousands of distinct cache keys over the run through varied q strings, pages or letter case), not a short fixed list, and the run explains why: the result cache in internal/catalog/search.go (Catalog.cache) is keyed by the raw query and page and never evicts, so a handful of repeated queries fills it within seconds and cannot reproduce the growth. The run treats the cache as the leading suspect the soak is to confirm or rule out, not as a cause already proven

The distinct queries return products the way real traffic does (built from catalogue words or names, as-typed prefixes, case or spacing variants, or pages that have results), not only random strings or numbers that match nothing: a cached empty result is a small fraction of the size of a cached page of products, so a soak of misses grows the heap far more slowly than qa's real traffic

The run weighs the incident note's suspicion of orders.MemoryStore (docs/incidents/2026-09-18-qa-search-oom.md) against the numbers instead of adopting it: at the 0.2 orders a second the note reports, orders add well under 1Mi an hour (a few hundred bytes each), far short of the about 21Mi an hour the note implies (70Mi at 07:40 to 256Mi at 16:15), so the order store cannot be the main source; the final message says so, and a soak may still include an orders phase to confirm it

The run tests the cache explanation against the incident's numbers before relying on it: it measures (locally, on an instance or in a test it runs itself) the heap a new cached search result costs when the query returns products, and multiplies by the incident's traffic (about 3 searches a second with about 70% of query strings new) to show whether the cache accounts for roughly the observed 21Mi an hour, stating the result either way; asserting the cache is the cause with no such check does not pass

The soak separates the suspects so the result says which one grows: search phases or runs with no orders (orders.MemoryStore keeps every order, so orders mixed into the search load would muddy the signal), and a control of repeated queries that should stay flat, or an equivalent comparison; a single mixed load whose rising memory could come from either store does not pass

The soak records the service's memory over time while it runs, by sampling /debug/vars (expvar memstats such as HeapInuse, HeapAlloc or Sys) or the qa pod's working set at regular intervals into a file or the test output, and each sample carries something that shows a restart (a counter such as TotalAlloc or NumGC that only grows, the process start, or the pod restart count), so an OOM-kill mid-run is not read as memory levelling off; a soak that only checks latency and error thresholds does not pass

The run says how to read the result against the qa pod's memory budget: what trend after warm-up indicates a leak, expressed against the 256Mi limit in deploy/qa/values.yaml or the incident's climb from about 70Mi to 256Mi (for example Mi an hour set beside the incident's roughly 21Mi an hour, or hours until the pod would reach 256Mi). A leak rule that is only a slope threshold chosen from local noise, with no relation to the limit or the observed climb, does not pass

The run estimates how much memory the soak should add at its default rate and duration (from a local measurement of the cache or from the incident's observed rate and traffic) and that estimate is large against heap noise and a real fraction of 256Mi; a soak whose default settings would add only a few Mi over the night, with no estimate, does not pass

The soak is not configured to abort on a latency threshold breach before the memory evidence is collected, since a pod slowing down as its heap grows is part of what the run is meant to capture; aborting when nearly every request fails (for example a wrong key) is fine

The soak rate is stated with a traffic source (the incident note's about 3 searches a second on qa, or the normal day's 6 checkouts a second from HLD section 7, about 12 searches a second) and stays within 20 requests a second per API key (ADR-0003) or spreads over enough keys; a rate justified only as headroom under the limiter does not pass

The final message says that qa is scaled to zero from 22:00 to 07:30 IST by the qa-scale-down schedule (.gitlab-ci.yml, ADR-0004), naming the hours or the schedule, so an overnight run needs that schedule paused (and the platform channel told) or must run within the day window; the run does not itself change the schedule

If the run adds a CI job for the soak, its timeout exceeds the soak's duration (the pipeline default in .gitlab-ci.yml is 1h), it is started by hand and it targets qa only; a run that adds no CI job passes, and so does one that says the 1h default rules out running it from CI
internal/catalog/search.go and internal/orders/orders.go are unchanged: the request is to prove the source, not to fix it; proposing a fix in the final message is fine

Existing files under deploy/ and cmd/ and the schedules in .gitlab-ci.yml are unchanged, and no new file under deploy/ changes qa (no raised memory limit, no replica change); new files that hold the soak tool itself are fine
No file the run writes defaults its target to the production host api.shopfront.example.net, and nothing in the run sends a request to it
The final message gives the command to start the soak against qa and says where the memory samples and any latency results end up

The run says the soak was not run against qa (qa is not reachable from this machine) and reports no qa memory or latency figures; figures from a local instance the run started itself are fine when they are clearly labelled as local

`make check` passes when the grader runs it in the output repository, and it does not run the soak or send traffic to any host outside the test process (an in-process test server inside a unit test is fine)
The run makes no git commit: the output repository's history still ends at the fixture commit and the changes are left in the working tree
No file written or edited contains an em dash character
